text:
Reads select authorized rows by id, predicate or search text.
Add an order, page size and cursor to browse a population.

State the rows, then the order and page. `messages where .roomId = roomId
last 20 by .at after c` means the newest matching messages. The compiler
chooses the index. Positional keys select identity for `id`/same-table references,
otherwise the declared unique key accepting types in order; ambiguous types need named columns.
The rules run before any projection, count or order reaches the caller.

For a table, order keys after `id` are redundant and omitted: `by .id, .at`
uses the same index and cursor as `by .id`. View orders retain later keys,
because distinct branches may carry the same source id; branch identity
breaks any remaining tie.

Unpaged aggregates infer a range seek only when its endpoint is already
present and cannot fail. Bounds requiring a short-circuit guard remain row
filters. A named id pin keeps its single-row access path and filters.

Finite ranked windows enumerate inclusive UTC buckets:
`bucket(lower) ..= bucket(upper)`. The exact endpoint comparisons still
filter every row. A missing finite upper bound stays a metered residual scan;
N_SPARSE_FILTER suggests `and .at <= now` when that is the intended window.
Paging by a maintained order key such as `.likeCount` is not a snapshot:
changes can move rows across a saved position. Restart to see the new order.
Value lanes deduplicate values; each lane keeps its source rule. Null never
becomes an index pin. When a membership list includes null, one ordinary
filtered lane reads the null-valued rows under the same rule.
A keyed `exists` inside `where` probes one authorized row per candidate;
when its discovery prefix cannot decide the other table's read rule, the
planner retains those probes and the certificate names the skipped rows.
A cut during discovery or while any lane head is unknown is incomplete and
has no cursor. A full page never certifies a prefix of an unfinished lane list.

A full positional unique key can be followed by named tests on that row:
`members[org, viewer, role = 'admin']`. The prefix must identify one declared
unique key; inferred indexes never resolve positions. E_QUARRY_KEY_ORDER
means a positional component followed a named one: move all positional
components first, then write the named tests.

Every ready `Read` carries `cut: 'meter' | 'words' | null` beside `complete`,
on the server and either device store. An empty page with `cut: 'meter'`
means partial: retry narrower, or continue if `next` exists; never "no matches".
`words` means the first term expanded past 32 words in an admitted non-uniform scope: narrow that
term or use scoped search (guide search). If both limits cut, `meter` wins.
Device reads and uniform server reads keep precise reasons.
Non-uniform server reads report `cut: null`: the reason is withheld, with `complete: false` still truthful.
`null` means "not disclosed here", not "not cut"; it also covers a horizon,
missing coverage. For `complete: false` with
`cut: null`, render "Results may be incomplete", even when empty; never "no matches".
A complete empty page has `cut: null` and `complete: true`.
Same-key observations retain their last answer marked `revalidating` during
plain refetch, reconnect and transport failure. Omitted `keep` and `keep: true`
share this policy; `keep: false` withdraws immediately. Inserts and non-policy updates retain through retries; deletes, policy-input changes and unknown evidence start a nonrenewable one-second bound. Bounded failure/timeout withdraws; replacements can still publish.
A notified cut keeps older replica answers ineligible until sync publishes it.
A whole server answer at that cut may replace sooner. Expiry, sign-out,
credential, store, schema and generation resets still withdraw immediately.
`fresh` and `since` describe server freshness, independently of revalidation.
With `keep: true`, a watch also lingers for 30 seconds after its last subscriber
leaves, sharing the same observation, expiry, invalidation and reset fences.
Local commits still revalidate it while unmounted; account/backend changes,
`clear_rows`, `settle_exit`, ephemeral resets and close end its authority.
See `guide client` for the complete retention and screen-lifetime recipe.
A ready list read always carries an array; an absent point can still be null.
`usePage` returns `items: []` while its first page is loading; earlier pages
remain visible while a later page is unavailable.

For device reads, online fallback asks only for missing facts or unknown presence.
Meter/word cuts and cursorless pages stay local, as do held queries and retained left groups.
Predictable pending writes block server fallback for dependent reads; unknown prediction
footprints block every query. Unrelated writes do not block. Withheld speculation
(past-horizon totals, extrema or points) stays `loading`; local cuts stay partial.
For one-shots, see `guide client`.
Keep a screen query locally complete (`snapback4 why <query>`); put server-needing
decorations in their own query so the main list never waits on them.
Keep the screen shell and draft mounted; render current reads.

A read denied by a table's rule answers as an empty page, not a refusal,
and a client cannot tell it apart from an empty readable page — by design,
so that a hidden row cannot be probed. For access UI, use a membership query
the viewer may read, such as a conversation lookup readable by its members:
a member gets the conversation even when its message page is empty.
An explicit `require … else CODE` still refuses with the program's code.

Named equalities covering a total unique key read one row and check any extra
columns there: `t[key = x, col = y]` returns null on a mismatch, and
`exists t[key = x, col = y]` returns false. Named equalities covering no
unique key plan an ordinary authorized scan.
Positional keys select identity for `id`/same-table references, otherwise one
declared unique key accepting the types in order. Ambiguous types need named
keys. Generated planning indexes never participate.
An explicit `by <authoredIndex>` keeps its existing point or prefix meaning.

References keep their table identity: `replies[id = r]` with `r: replies`
reads a reply, while `replies where .postId = p first 20 by .id` with
`p: posts` reads its replies. Using a reference to a different table as this identity
refuses; a declared unique reference column can accept it; a generic `id` does not carry that table-identity check.
An absent, hidden or null point target returns null. A predicate read returns
a page, empty when no visible row matches. A reference does not prove existence.
`snapback4 why <operation>` shows each read's source site, selected index,
column/key bindings, result form and selection reason; the same facts appear
in `check --json` execution sites. These are binder facts, not measured work.
For an expiring table, return the deadline with each row:

Held device observations republish at `nextExpiry`, including offline; render
those rows directly. Timers follow the row's deadline; a suspended page or a
busy host can delay the callback.
Only server-answered reads need a render-deadline filter to hide a returned
row while its next network answer is pending. Return `expiresAt`, as above.
In React, `useNow(deadline)` owns the timer and responds to clock estimates:

Render the rows returned by `useExpiringRows(rows)`. `client.now()` estimates the server's time and never
moves backward; `null` never expires. The hook cleans up on unmount.

For typing and viewing indicators, use an ephemeral table (`guide ephemeral`,
also `guide typing`). Keep its server query separate from the device-held
chats list. The expiring-rows recipe above is for durable disappearing messages.

The first read examples use the language card's tables. A page's read rule is checked
once when the prefix decides it, else per row, and a page whose rule still depends
on a column the scan does not pin is never `complete` (N_NEVER_COMPLETE names
the missing equality columns and an existing compatible index when one is
available). Keep the current equality prefix when adding those pins; choosing
a conversation narrows the answer to that scope. This is author guidance,
not a `check --fix` repair, and it does not change the read rule. With a total unique `(chatKey, principal)`
key on t, `.principal = viewer or exists t[.chatKey, viewer]` is decided by
the chat alone because the row is its own witness, so a roster page pinned
by the chat is complete and no second table is needed. An aborting mutation
page costs one examined unit before its verdict, plus its rule probes on
both true and false verdicts; a true verdict then examines candidates.
A page verdict evaluated from its pinned prefix charges the rule's static probe count on either outcome, including probes skipped by `and`/`or` short-circuiting.
A point read reserves that same static allowance before its lookup, equally
for a readable row, a hidden row and a miss. If it cannot pay, authorization
has no verdict and the answer remains incomplete. A device's trusted held
row needs no authorization probes.
A read states its predicate, search text, page size, order and continuation:
`t where predicate matching q last 20 by .at after c`. Omit parts the read
does not need. `first` ascends; `last` descends; id breaks ties. Predicates run
after the source rule. Parenthesize a nested read with its own modifiers:
`exists (messages[roomId = .roomId] matching q)`. The named inner key binds
the outer row's room; inside a predicate, `.` denotes that predicate's row.

Inside `where`, an ordering comparison (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) with a nullable
column of that row is false when the column is null. `.due < now` therefore
selects overdue tasks without a guard or a default. On the first order key it
is a seek when its endpoint is already present and cannot fail; a nullable
upper-only seek starts exclusively above null. `= null`
and `!= null` keep their ordinary meaning. Optional arguments and locals,
and comparisons outside `where`, still need a presence guard.
An endpoint behind a guard, such as `d != 0 and .due > 10 / d` or
`x != null and .due < x` for optional `x`, stays in the residual predicate,
even with `by .due`. The guard runs before that comparison. Present literals,
`now`, required parameters and arithmetic proven not to overflow can seek.
Parenthesized predicates also work before a named shape.

For a required enum with at most eight variants, `.status != 'done'` opens
the same pinned value lanes as `.status in ['todo', 'doing']`. A bound value
can also select the excluded variant. Fallible expressions remain residual
predicates so their guards still run first. Nullable enums retain a residual
inequality, including null rows; larger enums also stay residual.
Value lanes are chosen only when every lane's prefix decides the source read
rule. Otherwise both `!=` and `in` remain residual filters on one scan, which
can continue through visible rows with `next`; the non-uniform read still
reports `complete: false`.

Optional filters `(status = null or .status = status)` (also `==`, either order)
choose an indexed plan for each presence combination; reset the cursor when
filters change, and inspect each variant with `check --cost`.
At most three optional inputs expand; N_OPTIONAL_FILTER_LIMIT names any extra
residual filters, which can stay metered or move into separate queries.
For mutation population loops and top-level job sweeps, put the optional
condition inside an ordinary capped loop or stable sweep; a presence-selected
read cannot supply that loop domain.

`check --cost` displays the residual that still tests each visible candidate,
including `in` when another predicate supplies the lanes. A predicate fully
extracted into pins or lanes has no residual-skip clause. These explanations
do not change read rules, meter bounds or completeness.

N_NO_CURSOR: a returned page cannot continue. If the screen pages,
declare `c: cursor ?` and page with `after c`, preserving its predicate and order.

Filling `first N` or `last N` is complete without `next`. Composed fields
omit this note. Meter cuts, undecided authorization and missing device
coverage still apply (`guide reads`).

A boundless domain read uses the schema cap in ascending order, even in
nested shapes and mutation loops. A cap above the examined ceiling requires
explicit pagination for a returned page. `first N` remains an ordinary page;
`last N` remains the descending spelling.

`count(messages where .roomId = roomId)` and `sum(orders where .owner =
viewer, .amount)` stream their domains. They authorize and filter each row,
then release it. They do not retain a page of bodies. A meter cut or unknown
device coverage leaves the client observation `loading`, never a partial total.
Use a maintained view for a total that should be updated with each write.
`count(page)` still counts only that page.
An unpaged aggregate keeps enum inequalities and membership predicates as
residual filters on its streaming scan. It does not turn them into a bounded
merge page: `count(tasks where .status != 'done')` and
`sum(tasks where .status in ['todo', 'doing'], .n)` return either the whole
authorized total or null on interruption. Scan admission remains unchanged.

`exists messages where .roomId = roomId` stops at a visible match. It accepts
predicates and seeks, but no page clause or cursor. A visible or held witness
proves existence (`true`); absence needs full coverage: an interrupted or
undecided scan answers nothing. Mutations keep their ordinary scan
admission; rule probes keep exact-key semantics.

Finite ranked windows use inclusive UTC buckets from the lower through the
upper bound. Exact endpoints still filter rows. An `in` predicate over a list
or a read's column opens one ruled scan per distinct non-null value; a null
value adds one authorized null-filtered scan for a nullable column. Unknown
or cut discovery cannot certify the page. Use `check --cost` to inspect these
plans. Unknown widths print `lanes ≤ meter`; the author writes no lane list.

A resumable read-meter cut after every required head is known can carry `next`
after its last fully shaped emitted row, subject to final-answer eligibility.
Heap exhaustion clears the whole page and leaves the client observation `loading`, with no continuation,
even during the drain. Step exhaustion aborts; output exhaustion can refuse.
A uniform matching scan is always lazy. Opening and word-limit cuts cannot
supply continuation. A terminal full page need not carry `next`. Following a
cursor does not clear earlier incompleteness in `usePage`.

A direct table or maintained-view cursor binds the evaluated prefix and active
generation. Another prefix or schema adoption refuses it. Ordinary writes keep
it valid, but a changing order can move rows across the cursor. Refresh a live
ranking; continuation is not a snapshot. Planned unions preserve branch and
source-row identity, even when two tables contain the same id.

A top-level returned shape carries its page's `next`. A shaped row that cannot
finish is dropped with later rows; continuation reaches the unfinished visible
row first. If the same first shape cannot fit on retry, E_SHAPE_EXCEEDS_METER
refuses instead of repeating an empty page forever. Narrow its nested reads
or move expensive components into separate queries. Non-uniform reads cannot
reveal a hidden continuation position. Independent pages in one object each
need their own continuation owner; one cursor cannot cover lost siblings.
`sort` and `group` operate on their input page and retain that page's coverage.

A mutation classified `predicts: "never"`, from a server site or an author's
`: server` marker, may iterate a bounded plain prefix page when its read rule
is uniform over the prefix. `matching` and merges are refused for every
mutation page (`E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT`). Expiring scans follow the server
read-only-phase rule in guide programs. Prediction still needs a complete
schema-capped group: `for m in members where .roomId = roomId:` takes its bound from the
schema cap, so changing the cap changes every whole-group read. An explicit
`first <cap>` stays legal; a smaller explicit bound still fails the prediction
proof. A job's inner loop may also read a capped group without restating it.
Every page a mutation reads, including a page it only
binds, must be uniformly decided by its prefix (`E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT`): read it in
a query, or pin the deciding columns.
A page verdict evaluated from its pinned prefix charges the rule's static probe count on either outcome, including probes skipped by `and`/`or` short-circuiting; an aborting mutation page also costs one examined unit before the verdict.
The pass is atomic and remains subject to 1,024 rows written per mutation.
`check --cost` names the examined ceiling and, for expiring scans, the
unswept-row backlog and atomic `E_BOUND` outcome. It never commits a partial pass after a budget abort.

A job may put a read-only prelude before its first sweep. It runs again
at the start of every chunk, with its bindings visible there and its work
charged to that chunk's meter. Writes belong inside the sweep body.

Arguments use column types; `c: cursor ?` is an opaque optional cursor.
An omitted optional argument is null. `walk rooms[roomId] up .parentId depth 8`
returns the seed and at most eight parent hops. List operations and helpers
are on `guide language` and `guide shapes`; writes are on `guide writes`.

Web queries and predictions trust the backend compiler's structural admission;
the server rechecks submitted mutations. Local argument, row, rule, coverage
and runtime budget checks still run. A hand-built or corrupted backend can
therefore differ from a native device's structural refusal (`guide prediction`).

A bounded list loop that only reads, computes and emits may iterate a list
column, an alias, a helper result or a filtered/shaped list from a page.
It need not preserve the whole group. If its body writes rows, including
inside helpers or nested loops, the original `E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT` check
still applies. Every mutation page still needs a uniform plain prefix over
a table admitted by the expiry rule (guide programs); the meter and its
ceilings are unchanged.

To inspect a real account's server work under loopback `dev`, use the online
client `createClient({ url, session })` (or a bearer `token`); meters are available by default.
Successful `query` and `observe` answers include `Read.meter`:
`{ examined, indexEntries, probes, steps, heapBytes, outputBytes, rowsWritten, cut }`.
`Read.meter.cut` keeps the precise reason even for a non-uniform server read;
it is `meter`, `words` or null, with `meter` winning when both limits cut.
These are the engine's counters for that answer, not latency or process memory;
`probes` is rule_probes and `heapBytes` is charged heap work. A local fallback
keeps its previous answer’s counters only until the fetch settles. Local device reads
have no meter; use the online client to inspect the server for the same account.
`meter: true` and `x-snapback-meter: 1` on `POST /q/<op>` remain explicit forms.
Loopback dev includes the field without either; `serve` ignores the header and never returns
meters. The counters can reflect hidden work and are development-only.
`snapback4 run <op> '<json args>' --as <principal id> --json` also prints
the engine's `metered` counters against `.snapback4/store.sqlite`.
A declared persona such as `alice` resolves to `dev:alice`; any other `--as`
value is used verbatim (including `user:...`, `member:42` and `dev:alice`).
The default is `dev:alice`. Jobs still run as the system.

Declare `query name(..) held:` for a device-only answer. `check --verbose` prints
`runs: device (held; server refuses E_QUERY_HELD; no server fallback)`.
`dev`, `serve` and `run` refuse it with E_QUERY_HELD and a guide search rewrite;
the local clients answer from held rows, online or offline, without server
fallback even at a horizon or cut. With horizon-free sources, `check --verbose` reports
horizon-free source coverage. Answer completeness still depends on runtime
authorization and limits; the marker does not acquire rows.
An unscoped search through expiring memberships can remain non-uniform and
incomplete below every limit. A full `first 1` page is complete without a cursor. Read `complete` on each answer; a held query with an
online-only source or no read sites gets no source-coverage line.
Sources include reads nested in expressions such as the search text after `matching`.
For full server history beyond holdings, use the grouped or newest form on the search card.

E_QUARRY_POSITIONAL_SCAN means the argument types do not identify one declared
unique key, or a positional key would scan a population.

E_QUARRY_MODIFIER_SCOPE means a nested read's modifiers are ambiguous.
Parenthesize the inner read, for example `exists (messages[roomId = .roomId]
matching q)`, and put the outer page's `by .roomId after c` after its predicate.

N_SEEK is advice for an older explicit-index read whose residual filter can
seek. For a new read, write `messages where .roomId = roomId and .at >= start
first 20 by .at after c`; the planner makes that comparison a seek.

Mutations insert, update and delete rows in one transaction.
Rules and constraints apply before that transaction commits.

If `messageId` in `writeForms` addresses retained history from a room the
writer has left, the call still predicts. Reads hide the updated message
because current membership is absent, while readable inserts remain visible.
Unknown reaction authority also hides that provisional reaction.
See `guide prediction` for authorization on each device read.

For replay adapters and retry-safe intents, pass a `mintId()` you stored with
the intent, or name a fixture label with `idFrom("post-17")`: the same label
gives the same valid id on every client and host, so a replay needs no ledger.
`idFrom` also names fixture rows; derived ids sort before every minted id.
Pass it as `{ id }`; a retry returns the original outcome and never applies twice:
`client.mutate(api.send, args, { id })`. The id must have the `mintId()` form:
26 uppercase Crockford base32 digits (0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ), with
the first digit 0–7; malformed ids return local `failed` with `E_WRITE_ID`.
Mint once and keep the id with the intent. It identifies the write, not a row;
prediction still mints separate row ids through `new_ids`.
A retry of a pending write on the same client returns the same Write object;
a settled retry returns its retained receipt, without historical result values.
Online, web and native clients share this rule; a recovered queued write is
reused before prediction or admission. Already-open owners of one device store
compare and admit under its transaction: equal input reuses the original entry
and row ids, and conflicting input changes nothing, even during a send. `client.write(id)` and
`usePendingWrite(op, id)` observe that same id.

Reusing an id with different operation names or JSON arguments returns local
`E_WRITE_ID_REUSE` while the client knows the input: unresolved submissions,
its last 256 terminal input identities, or its recovered outbox. Object key
order does not matter. This refusal does not replace the original write or emit
a terminal event for it. A receipt recovered after reopen holds no arguments,
so it returns the original outcome without comparing inputs. When neither
outbox nor receipt knows an id, the request reaches the server: its record is
keyed by principal and mutation id, and an existing record wins even if the
operation or arguments differ. Use a new id for a new intent. A client remembers
used ids for its lifetime (ids only after the bounded input/receipt window);
if a known id has lost its receipt and left the outbox, it refuses
`E_WRITE_RECEIPT_EXPIRED` instead of admitting it again. Reopen to recover that
outcome through the server. The server guarantee belongs to that backend store.
An online `createApp` journal separately preserves ids retired after a store
change, including sent ids displaced to make room for retirement receipts,
so reopening cannot replay those writes on the replacement store:
evicted bodies return `E_WRITE_RECEIPT_EXPIRED` without dispatch. It keeps up to
4,096 compact retirement ids; saturation durably blocks new admissions until
the application reconciles prior outcomes and explicitly replaces that journal,
rather than forgetting ids automatically. Already-admitted intents remain
recoverable as pending while their outcomes are unresolved.
Online intent records its dispatch store before transmission. A failed receipt
save preserves the known terminal outcome for mutate, lookup and notification;
reopening may resend that intent only to the acknowledging store, whose replay
record prevents double execution. Persisted terminal receipts are not reposted.
A replacement retires old-store intent with an unknown-outcome refusal; an old
unbound intent may replay only to the first store its journal has seen.
For a caller-supplied id with no local outcome, a prediction or validation refusal
queues the write without a row so the server can answer from its replay record.
The journal preserves this replay eligibility through navigation. If the server
has no record, it executes or refuses the write against its current state.
Separate live web tabs have separate outboxes; the server deduplicates their
requests under the same principal and id. Different principals may use the same
id independently.

Writes that do not predict show pending with `usePendingWrite(op)` from
`snapback4/react`: `run(args)` submits, `pending` covers submission through
terminal `sent` or `failed`, and `last` is the Write. `run(args, { waitSeconds: 0 })`
returns at custody; disable submission only with `inFlight`, never `pending`. Keep its mutation id in
view state; `usePendingWrite(op, savedId)` resumes observation after reload
without submitting again. `client.write(id)` reads the kept outcome (undefined
for an unknown id or an evicted id that has left the outbox); `onWrite` reports
later terminal changes. The ordinary in-memory history retains at most 256 terminal outcomes.
Failed receipt saves retain known summaries separately until persistence or close. The local client reads the device's one atomic window of the last
256 server terminal receipts and its current outbox directly, so another native
owner's settlement cannot leave a stale pending outcome. Reads and repeated
flushes do not refresh the window. Queued terminal writes emit at most once
per client, including through retirement and overlapping notifications. Lookups never emit.
Local receipts survive reopen. Before deleting an adopted web tab's store,
its terminal receipts enter a shared server/viewer window bounded to 256 in
recovery order. Existing shared ids keep their outcome and position. Openers
and `client.write(id)` read it alongside the device's own 256 receipts;
reads neither copy nor refresh it, so another tab's adoption cannot hide a
receipt from a reload. Outbox ownership stays exclusive: a held Web Lock is
never taken; a queued background lock request wakes recovery when its owner
releases it, and closing cancels the wait. Unidentified journals wait for a
matching open or sync signal. Persistence failures get at most three retries,
after 1, 2 and 4 seconds; later opens or sync signals can try again. Receipt
lookups do not create the shared window before adoption. Storage clearing or eviction
from both windows can make an id unknown. Recovered success carries `replayed: true`
and no result; recovered failure keeps code/family and `write refused: CODE`.
Refusals before durable admission, the raw online tier and mock remember ordinary
outcomes for their client lifetime only, up to 256 terminal outcomes.
Close completes after local work without waiting for the network. A mutation or
action keeps a response received before close completes; otherwise its caller
receives pending with its id. Late responses are consumed and discarded.
`createApp` and device mutation intent recover on reopen; raw online callers
retain their retry id, and action callers collect the same server action id.

`client.acquired` and `useAcquired()` report completed snapshot and catch-up
for the current store, stay true offline, and reset with invalidated acquisition.
The online tier has no partition and reports false. In an opener, use
`if (client.link() === "online") await client.sync()` before exposing a screen
that needs immediate offline predictions; skip the wait on an offline cold start.
If sync loses the link or the partition is refused, acquisition can remain false.
Network fetch failures resolve `sync()` without a value and set the link offline;
return the open client. Close and rethrow only unexpected opener exceptions.
A Write queued without a row before acquisition carries
`reason: "queued without a row: not acquired yet"`; other missing local evidence
says `queued without a row: local data does not justify prediction`.
Predicted rows carry pending; a pending Write has no predicted result.

`upsert` set-state writes (likes, reactions and votes) predict updates of
rows the device holds. A missing row predicts an insert only when its synced
group is held with no horizon, both the key and the materialized insert image
prove readability, and the device holds every row that can collide on a
secondary unique index or count toward an affected cap. Defaults are part of
that image. Otherwise it queues without a predicted row, including in a left
group. See `guide prediction` for the conditions and a set-membership recipe.
An expiring cap limits live occupancy; unswept expired rows can require a
bounded recount. Held snapshots cannot prove server occupancy or recount cost.
Occupancy-increasing writes queue without predicted rows and settle on the
server even after full acquisition; updates within a cap group can still predict.
Replacing an expired same-id row also queues: the server may have swept it and
refilled the cap before sync reaches the device. A held live row can still
support an update within its cap group.

NOT_FOUND means a point write has no target, or a write to an unreadable target
was refused without disclosing its existence. It is also the conventional
application code for `row ! else NOT_FOUND`. Check a readable target and retry;
do not infer absence from a refused blind write.

An alternate-key delete of a missing row refuses `NOT_FOUND` locally when the
synced group proves absence; otherwise it queues for server resolution.

For `after insert <- exists t[key]`, a local hit satisfies the postcondition.
A local miss predicts `E_CONSTRAINT` only when the key proves readability
and its synced group is fully held without a horizon. Otherwise either an
ordinary insert or an upsert queues without a predicted row; the server
decides the postcondition when the write arrives.

Defaults fill missing insert columns on the writing host, including the insert
branch of `upsert`; updates and existing-row upserts never reapply defaults.
`upsert` inserts or patches: on an existing row, unnamed columns keep their
values. An incomplete insert patch answers `NOT_FOUND`. An explicit null
clears an optional column. Omitted asset columns keep their placement; an explicit
asset id on a row you cannot read must be your own upload, even if it equals the
retained id. The update
rule runs before asset diagnostics. Conditional `if` sees old only inside
the engine; neither old nor the merged image is a program binding.

For update/upsert, "readable" means the read rule admits the old row in the
pre-write state, before the patch or any of its effects. The engine resolves
id and unique-key targets privately; the update rule judges old and next.

E_INPUT means an argument or row value does not fit its declared type.
Correct the named field or its declaration. A typed reference never reads its
target; use `require exists t[id] else CODE` to require a visible target.

E_CONFLICT means a conditional update found that the row changed.
The refusal carries the current row only when its read rule admits the viewer.
Read it and retry with a fresh edit.

E_QUARRY_WRITE_TESTS means a write target includes tests beyond its unique
key. For a readable row, write `require exists members[org, viewer, role =
'admin'] else NOT_ADMIN`, then `update members[org, viewer] { role: 'member' }`.
Choose the refusal code for your application. This explicit check refuses a
hidden or missing row and grants no write authority; the compiler does not
insert it automatically.

| Target before the write | Refusal details |
| --- | --- |
| Readable | `E_RULE`; `E_CONFLICT` with a read-rule `current`; named `E_CONSTRAINT`; `E_INPUT` |
| Unreadable or absent | `NOT_FOUND` for rule denial, an `update` condition, secondary unique clash, or an incomplete insert patch; no row, index, column or branch detail |

A hidden collision on ordinary insert or `insert ... if absent` stays
`E_RULE`; a readable collision names its index (if-absent returns null).
An update or upsert-patch colliding with a different hidden row returns generic
`E_RULE` when its target is readable and `NOT_FOUND` when its target is unreadable.
Use `upsert counters[recipient] { count: 1 }` under an `update` rule to
write another principal's row. Success discloses the admitted row's existence
and the update rule predicates. It grants no extra stream or snapshot row.
A condition belongs on `update`; an upsert inserts or patches. A condition
needs a row you can read; a blind patch needs none. On a row you cannot read,
immutable columns in a patch are ignored. A readable immutable mismatch still
names the column. Before target lookup, the engine reserves room for the rule
probes and the largest merged image allowed by the schema and supplied patch;
if it cannot fit, `E_BOUND` refuses equally for a hidden or absent target.
Delete targets and insert/if-absent collision lookups also reserve authorization
before resolving a row, including expired rows. The allowance covers the read
rule's worst case, including probes that could short-circuit; execution still
charges the rule work once.

The table names are the language card's. A final write is the implicit
return; bind one to use its row (`row = insert ..`). Writes check the rule,
then unique indexes, caps, immutable columns, text formats and `after
insert` postconditions; any refusal rolls the whole mutation back, and a
maintained aggregate is written through its source rows. Every written row
fans out to its partitions (guide sync). A mutation applies at most once
per client-minted id and principal. Valued updates/upserts and conflict
`current` are ordinary read-rule gets (null or withheld when hidden), evaluated
at the read's state; a write that grants read authority may return its row.

The recorded body is the replay body, with value-free diagnostic messages
and no `result` or `current`. Retries return only
execution identity (`sent`/`failed`, `seq`/`why`, `replayed`), withholding
historical `result` and `current`, including scalar results after a lost reply.

On the web, admission waits for the IndexedDB commit; pagehide or becoming
hidden sends only the oldest unconfirmed write with keepalive, including a retry
of that same head if an ordinary send is in flight when the page exits.
A blocked or oversized head is never skipped; clients share
the browser's 64 KiB body budget. Unsent/unconfirmed writes stay durable for retry on reopen with
the same mutation id, so replay cannot apply a write twice.
If an exit response has not finished after one second, ordinary flushing
retries that same durable head before advancing; an unknown outcome never
skips a write. `close()` stops waiting immediately without cancelling the
keepalive request.
An admission that finishes while the page is suspended rechecks the exit
transport after its commit; on reopen, a matching server store identity and
non-regressed head allow unknown writes to replay before the first sync finishes.
With an exclusive persistence claim, the web device records the mutation id, operation,
arguments and minted row ids synchronously in localStorage, in call order,
before `mutate` returns its promise. Same-origin navigation can therefore leave before IndexedDB admission
commits: the next client admits those records before new writes, then sends
through the ordinary outbox with the original ids. A closed tab's records are
adopted by the next device that opens the store, under the outbox's exclusive claim.
Adoption runs with that device's first sync, so a receipt from a closed tab
answers `client.write(id)` once that sync completes, not at the moment it opens.
Recovery and new admissions take submission numbers from the same device counter;
already-queued writes precede recovered orphan records. A matching orphan waiting
for backend adoption installs the destination's authenticated backend first. An
orphan missing its kept backend is skipped with its journal intact until a
later matching open can establish ownership; a broken orphan does
not prevent healthy stores from opening.
Recovered records stay bound to their original backend store identity; a
replacement retires them without sending them to the new backend.

The journal allows at most 32 records and 256 KiB of UTF-8 keys and values per
device store, and 64 KiB per record. A browser call that cannot synchronously
keep its intent refuses `E_ADMISSION` with a site and rewrite: no new intent
is accepted. Its promise is already fulfilled with `failed`, and exposes
`state`, `id` and `why` in the calling stack. Missing restored identity,
unavailable/full storage, an exhausted journal, or
an app that cannot journal therefore cannot silently lose a click.
Use `webDevice()` and `localStorageSessionStore()`, wait for readiness or repair
storage, then retry the original id. Browser storage clearing after admission
can still erase the journal.

A destination must open
a client to recover a record that never reached the outbox; keepalive remains
best-effort and sends only admitted writes. Built-in IndexedDB requires Web
Locks and refuses opening without them. Custom persistence must provide an
exclusive claim and discoverable alternate stores; see the client reference.
Recovered executable records keep successful predictions, but local refusals
queue for the server to decide, so stale rows cannot permanently cancel them.
For programmatic navigation, `await client.mutate(...)` before navigating
is the strongest durable boundary; handle a `failed` outcome before leaving.
`pending` means IndexedDB custody is durable and the server outcome still
needs confirmation. A write-specific admission refusal returns the ordinary failed
outcome and removes its journal record, replaces it with a non-executable
cancellation, or acknowledges it in IndexedDB. If both stores reject cancellation,
the recovery outcome is indeterminate: the executable record can survive and a
later recovery can admit it if the authored condition changes. The returned
refusal alone does not guarantee preserved cancellation in that case.
A device write-target miss that cannot prove the insert conditions above
queues without a predicted row and still sends `/m`.

A reference column accepts any id string and never
reads its target: when a mutation needs a visible target, guard first —
`require exists prompts[promptId] else PROMPT_NOT_FOUND` — a metered point
read that is false for an absent or hidden row; deleting a target neither
deletes nor refuses the rows that reference it, so a lifecycle is the
application's, in its mutations and rules.

An `exists` or `count` check sees only rows its viewer may read. It cannot
prevent a clash with another guest's private booking. E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT
refuses a mutation domain whose read rule is not decided by its scope.
Use one row per occupied night and let `unique` enforce the constraint for
every writer. Insert the booking and its nights in the same mutation:

`firstDay` and `lastDay` are calendar-day numbers in the app's chosen calendar;
the last day is excluded. A second guest reserving an occupied night gets
`TAKEN`, and the entire mutation rolls back, including any earlier free nights.
The normal write and work meters bound the loop; exceeding them also rolls
back the mutation. This example only books nights; cancellation must release
its nights in the same transaction as cancelling the booking.

The availability table is deliberately public: a named unique refusal applies
only when the clashing row is readable. A hidden collision stays `E_RULE`,
even with `else TAKEN`. Use this example only if occupied dates and booking
references may be public. Private booking details keep their own read rule.
If the product instead permits readable availability checks, an `exists` or
`count` domain over that public availability table has a uniformly readable
audience. Pinning a private guest merely narrows the check; it cannot enforce
a constraint across all guests.

For timestamp order with ties, use existing columns: `sync last 500 by .at, .id`
and query `last 50 by .at, .id`. No ordinal or conversation-row rewrite is needed.

Pass the returned `next` as `c` to page newest first by ordinal. Reusing the
mutation id on retry neither increments again nor inserts twice. This short
shared-history example is online-only and only members can advance its counter;
private conversations also need membership read rules. If you sync and predict it, a local ordinal is provisional until the
server commits and reconciles concurrent sends.

`old` in a rule and the conditional update's `if` are evaluated inside the
engine. An update/upsert result and conflict `current` are read-rule gets,
never the merged patch image: null or withheld when hidden at that read.
A patch can grant read authority and then return its row. Omitted asset columns
keep their placement. An explicit asset id on a row you cannot read must be your
own upload, even if it equals the retained id. Update authority is checked
before asset diagnostics. A readable aggregate view is an explicit delta read channel;
`N_MAINTAIN_DELTA` notes potentially wider source update authority.

A missing `upsert` predicts its insert when the synced group is held with no
horizon, both the key and the materialized insert image prove readability,
and the viewer-readable partition covers every secondary unique lookup and
affected cap group. The image includes key columns, patch and defaults; a
whole-table cap needs the whole public table. Left groups and unproved
conditions queue without a predicted row and still send `/m` (guide prediction).
`check --verbose` calls an upsert with an unprovable insert arm `predicts: conditional updates`,
and lists that arm in its summary with the first failing horizon, rule or cap
coverage proof. Updates need coverage for changed non-null unique keys and cap groups.
Unchanged keys/groups need no new proof. Expiring cap moves queue.
Residency explains each constraint. `insert ... if absent` reports the same insert limitation.
An id supplied to `insert ... if absent`, including a parameter or helper result,
needs the `byId` absence proof too. Only an id minted by `new` during the call
(including an omitted id) can use a covered secondary unique key instead.
`check` preserves a local's `new` fact across unrelated requires, reads, emits
and writes. A direct assignment tracks the local's new value; a branch or loop
that may assign it discards its fact. Other locals keep their mint facts.
Membership-scoped reactions with `last 500` cannot prove absence outside that
window; removing it still leaves `(messageId, principal)` unable to decide
`exists members[.conversationId, viewer]`. A viewer-keyed read rule with no
horizon and caps grouped by that viewer predicts a first write but shows only
the viewer's own reactions. Full public sync covers a per-message cap but
makes every reaction public. Membership reads can predict without a horizon
when every unique key and cap group includes `conversationId` and the device
holds the deciding membership row; that acquires all reactions in the held
conversation. None of these means complete children of just the held messages.
If no shape fits the product, this write queues until the server answers;
show its pending state using the returned write's `state` and `client.onWrite`
(guide writes). Changing `upsert` to an existence branch does not supply absence
or cap coverage.

The at-most-once record stores the replay body, with value-free diagnostic
messages and no `result` or `current`. Replay returns
execution identity only, with `replayed: true`; historical `result` and
`current` are withheld, including after revocation or a dropped response.
The same operation id under another principal has no access to that receipt.
`delete` keeps its own existing rule and behavior.

Queries read data; mutations change it in one transaction.
Jobs run background work, and helpers share logic between programs.

A mutation with `predicts: "never"` (a server site or `: server`) may pass
over a bounded plain prefix page whose read rule is uniform over its prefix,
without a complete schema-capped group. A `: server` mutation may scan an
expiring table only in its initial read-only statement prefix (guide programs);
its pages still need a uniform plain prefix, `matching` and merges stay refused,
and predicting mutations still cannot scan expiring tables. Move the scan into
that phase, or use a job sweep, which may read a table with expiry. A predicting mutation
keeps the complete-group requirement for page loops: `for row in t where .owner = viewer:`
uses the schema cap, without restating it. An explicit `first N` remains legal;
an explicit bound below the cap still fails that proof. A job's inner loop may
also read a capped group this way. A bounded list loop whose
body only reads, computes and emits may use a list column, alias, helper result,
or filtered/shaped list derived from a page; it need not preserve the whole group.
A row write anywhere in that body, including an inlined helper or nested loop,
keeps the original structural-fanout check and its capped-group rewrite.
Every page a mutation reads, even just
binding it, must be uniformly decided by its prefix (`E_STRUCTURAL_FANOUT`).
When a capped scope can decide the rule, the rewrite names the missing rule
columns and a capped loop that supplies their values. Pinning `.readerId` decides visibility; it grants no read
authority over another reader's inbox. See `guide feeds` for removal limits.
For `exists` and aggregate constraint checks without a deciding capped scope,
the refusal explains that hidden rows would be missed. Use a per-unit unique
constraint every writer obeys, or a readable availability audience if the
product permits it; `guide writes` has a per-night booking example. A hidden
unique collision stays E_RULE; only a readable collision can use its named code.
The pass is atomic and still aborts above 1,024 rows written. `check --cost`
prints the examined ceiling and, for expiry, the unswept-row backlog and
atomic `E_BOUND` outcome rather than a first-N-rows price.
For structural fanout, compiling and serving refuse it, and a native device checks again; the web device trusts that admission and does not repeat the check, so a hand-built or corrupted backend can still run there.

The table names are the language card's; a `job` is `for row in table where predicate:` sweeps (guide jobs), or `native`: the app's
own Rust, hosted as wasm; a `query` may be `native` too, run on the server
as the viewer and on a device over its rows (guide native). Operations in `schema.q`
are called by name (`api.thread`); operations in `snapback/feed.q` are
`api.feed.<name>`; jobs are not on api.ts. `require cond else CODE` refuses
with the program's own code, which reaches the client as `{ code, family:
"rule", .. }`; `CODE` is UPPER_SNAKE and never starts with `E_`. Statements
are `x = expr` (bind or reassign a local), `(a, b) = divmod(..)`, `require`, `if:`/`else if:`/`else:`, `for x in
domain:`, `break`, `continue`, `return`, a helper `fn` call, and a write; every other
expression must be bound or returned. `fn` takes one expression or a body ending
in `return expr` or a bare `return`; calls work in statements and expressions.
A helper return exits only the helper, and its locals cannot capture the caller's.
It never repositions or reclassifies an enclosing page.
Queries cannot write or mint ids, including through a helper; the call site names
the write that does not belong.

A backend shares one namespace of tables, shapes and helpers across `.q`
files. `snapback/schema.q` supplies root operations; `snapback/social.q`
supplies `api.social.<op>`. Import the generated `api` and use one client.
`sync` declares which devices hold rows and answer local reads; there are
no resolvers, migrations or subscriptions to manage.

**Two ways to run.** `snapback4 init` starts local-first: declare `sync` and
pass a device to `createApp` for offline data. `init --online` creates
`src/client.ts` without a device or `sync`; server queries stay live through
`/changes`. Both share rules, meters, identity, assets and jobs. Add a device
and `sync` later. `init --expo` selects native when available, online in Expo Go.
Starters, `check` and `dev` write `snapback/generated/package.json` with
`{"type":"module"}`: Node ESM seeds can import `api.ts` even in a CommonJS
app. Other scripts retain their module interpretation; Expo's `worker.mts`
explicitly uses ESM.

E_INTERNAL means the interpreter reached an undefined compiler temporary.
It names the operation and statement site, without exposing the generated
variable name as an input error. Recompile with `snapback4 check`; if it
recurs, report the operation and site as a compiler defect.

E_OP means the requested operation or route does not exist, or was called
through the wrong door. For example, `client.mutate(api.thread, args)`
cannot run a query; use `client.query(api.thread, args)`. Run
`snapback4 check` and use the generated API's module-qualified names.
Call actions with `client.act`; run jobs with `snapback4 run <job> '{}'`
or a schedule, since jobs are not client operations. Check the HTTP path
when the message instead names an unknown route.

E_OP_RESERVED means an application's refusal code starts with the
platform's reserved `E_` prefix. For example,
`require allowed else E_AUTH` must use
`require allowed else NOT_MEMBER`. Pick an UPPER_SNAKE application code
at the use site and handle that code on the client. The same rule applies
to a unique index's `else` hook; it does not require adding the code to the
platform registry.

E_QUARRY_PLACEMENT means a statement is valid only in another context.
For example, `query add():` cannot contain `insert notes { body: 'hello' }`;
make that operation `mutation add():` so the write runs in its transaction.
Queries cannot insert, update, delete or mint ids, even through a helper.
Keep read-only work in a query, put writes in a mutation or job, and put
`break` or `continue` inside the loop they control. The rewrite names the
misplaced statement and where it belongs.

E_EMIT_IN_QUERY means a query tried to enqueue an external effect.
For example, `query send():` cannot contain `emit notify { body: 'hello' }`;
declare `effect notify` and change the operation to `mutation send():`.
Call that mutation for the send intent. Queries may rerun to refresh a
screen, so they only read; mutations and jobs keep emitted effects in
their commit for a worker with a service token to perform (guide effects).
Moving the emit into a helper called by the query does not make it legal.

Quarry defines your tables, access rules and backend operations.
Queries and eligible mutations can run on devices that hold their inputs.

`snapback/schema.q` holds tables, views, shapes, helpers, programs and schedules
in any order. Other `.q` files share its namespace; their operations and scheduled
jobs use `<module>.<name>`. `check --fix` qualifies an unambiguous bare job name.
Comments start with `--`; blocks indent two spaces. The suite compiles every block.

Time arithmetic uses durations: `now + 1m` is one minute from now,
and `now - .at` is elapsed time; `day(now)`, `hour(now)` and `bucket(now, 2m)`
produce UTC calendar ordinals (`guide time`).

`createRoom` above predicts: its room is readable through the membership
inserted later in the same call. Reads authorize the current provisional
image against all pending writes. `edit` of retained history after leaving
the room also predicts, but the edited image is hidden until settlement.
See `guide prediction`.

Helpers expand at each call: a table-typed parameter keeps a row argument as a row (fields need no lookup), while a reference argument stays a reference.
An enum fits `text <=N` when every variant has at most N characters and
contains no control characters except tab, LF and CR. This is
static and total: no variant is truncated or converted at runtime. If one
variant is too long, declare the helper parameter with the enum instead.
After a scalar `where` predicate, a declared shape name shapes the page:
`where not .hidden card` and `where not .hidden { ...card }` agree. A valid
row/object shape inside a predicate keeps its meaning; parenthesize it to
make that scope explicit, or use `{ ...card }` explicitly for the page.

`t[id]` reads one row; positional composite keys require an unambiguous declared
unique key. Named keys select columns. `t where predicate first 20 by .at after c`
pages ascending; `last` descends, with id breaking ties. Optional filters use
`(status = null or .status = status)`; empty `matching q` browses in order.
`count`, `sum`, `min` and `max` stream domains. Min/max skip nulls and return null
for empty/all-null domains, otherwise the value's type. Their second argument
accepts scalar row expressions; `.field` binds that row and named locals remain
in scope. Move ambiguous enclosing-row references into a helper with named inputs.
Literal `.col` extrema seek the first visible matching non-null indexed value;
other expressions scan under meters (constant under a cap, growing otherwise). `check --cost` names the plan. A cut aggregate
is unavailable, including before `??`; devices need complete domain coverage.
Rules precede comparisons. `exists` stops at a visible match; unknown domains
cannot prove absence. See `guide reads`.

Values: `viewer` (a principal), `now` (a time; in a mutation it is the commit's
instant), `new` (an id, mutations only), `true`, `false`, `null`, integers,
`'text'` or `"text"` with `\n`, `\t` and `\\`, `[a, b]` (a bounded list),
`{ a, b: c }` (an object; a bare name is `name: name`). `=` and `!=` are total
(null equals null); `<` and friends, `+`, `-` and `*` need present operands:
narrow with `if x != null:`, `x ! else CODE`, `x ?? default`, or `require x
!= null else CODE`. Guards narrow fields of a bound row too, through `and`/`or`,
conditional arms and the paths that survive an early return; rebinding clears the fact. `time - time` is an int of milliseconds; `time + int` a
time. Text `+` concatenates two present texts. `count(text | page | list)` counts characters or items; `lower(text)`, `trim(text)`, `join(list, separator)`, `sum(page, .col)`, `sum(list)`, `min(a, b)`,
`max(a, b)`, `min(page, .col)`, `max(page, .col)` (also lists of rows), `slice(text | list, start, end)`, `sort(list, 'col', '-col')`,
`group(list, 'col')`, `first(list)`, `last(list)`, `at(list, index)` (element or null),
`tokens(text)`, `sha256(text)`, `share(amount, list, member)`, `(q, r) = divmod(a, b)`,
`(lo, hi) = sorted(a, b)`. `x = expr` binds or reassigns a local with a compatible type; reassignment resets its refinements. Arguments cannot be shadowed. A program ends
with `return [value]`, or with its last expression, or with its final write.
An inline ordered page needs parentheses to separate its order keys from
the column argument: `min((t first 20 by .at), .col)`. Binary `min(a, b)`
and `max(a, b)` retain their meaning; a collection followed by `.col` selects
the aggregate.
`xs = []` then `xs = xs + [value]` appends under the heap meter; `for x in xs:` can iterate the accumulated list.

`sha256` is for high-entropy capability tokens and content checksums. It hashes
the exact UTF-8 bytes without normalization and returns lowercase hexadecimal.
It is not password hashing, low-entropy email anonymization, a signature, a
MAC, or entropy generation; a digest is not automatically safe to publish.

`unique principal, day(at)` enforces calendar uniqueness. `search body`
declares word-prefix search. The planner builds indexes for predicates,
order, rule probes, sync, caps and expiry (`guide indexes`).

One `use server` in any module (`schema.q` is usual) enables the whole
project; repeating it is harmless. Actions, routes and schedules naming an
action require it. Effects (including secrets, retry, backoff, deadline and
cancellation), jobs, schedules naming a job and service seats need no directive.
This block extends the core schema above.

E_INIT_CONFLICT means `init` found files or package entries it would
overwrite, and wrote nothing. To add a starter beside your own files, rerun
with `--skip-existing`: every existing file (including `snapback/*.q`) is kept
exactly as it is and only the missing files are written. Beside a schema
without the starter's operations, the screen behind the sign-in is a `Home`
that compiles against any schema; replace it after `check`.
Otherwise rename the listed files, then rerun `snapback4 init --web` (or
`--expo`). Reconcile named package.json entries in either case. Never init
into another directory and copy it over yours: that overwrites your schema.
Unrelated files and symlinks can stay. An existing README.md stays intact;
the starter writes its setup instructions to README.snapback.md instead.

For a present row, `{ ...p, extra }` and `p { *, extra: extra }` contribute
the same columns and extra value. Shapes keep `*`; object fields and spreads
can replace inherited fields with an explicit field and its type, as `handle`
does above. Two explicit fields with the same name are refused.

E_QUARRY_SYNTAX means the parser could not read the form at the reported
file, line and column. For example, `query answer:` is missing its argument
parentheses: write `query answer():`, then indent `return 42` by two spaces
on the next line. Keep the colon, close each `(`, `[` and `{`, and separate
arguments and object fields with commas. Follow the diagnostic's rewrite;
`snapback4 check --fix` applies it only when marked mechanical. Fix the first
bad line and rerun `check`; a later empty-body error may be its consequence.

E_QUARRY_UNKNOWN means a name cannot be resolved in this scope: a local,
argument, table, column, index or helper may be misspelled or undeclared.
For example, after `message = 'hello'`, `return mesage` must be
`return message`. Check the declared spelling and the diagnostic's suggested
name; declare a missing local before using it. For a page, name its predicate and order: `posts where .authorId = viewer
last 20 by .at after c`. `snapback4 check --fix` applies only mechanical repairs.

- `while` and recursion → `for` over a page, list, `range(a, b)` with int expressions, or `tokens(text)`; `walk` for a chain.
- Floats → integer minor units in `decimal S` and `money CUR S`, or a native job.
- A typed map with dynamic keys → `group(list, 'col')`, whose result is a list of `{ key, items }` groups in first-seen order.
Before editing, `check --fix` verifies every compiled source; an editor save refuses the repair with its filename. Its final compile re-reads the project.

Ordinary field access propagates null: `row.body` is null when `row` is null.
`check --fix` removes only the `?` in `a?.b`, preserving the base expression
and evaluating it once, including when it is a call or read.

- Guessed spellings are refused with a canonical rewrite; `snapback4 check --fix` applies mechanical repairs (including missing indexes, argument `once`, repeated wildcard fields and empty operation parentheses): `cond ? a : b` → `a if cond else b`; `a?.b` → `a.b`; `elif` → `else if`; `proc` → `fn`; `//` and `#` → `--`; `==` → `=`.

Maintained columns put an aggregate on the row it describes. Their source
is ordinary and non-expiring. Omit `by` when exactly one source column references
the parent; otherwise name that reference explicitly. The
engine owns the column; a write result omits it. Read the row for its value.
Adding or redefining it recounts existing sources in atomic activation.
The event-free generation barrier makes devices reacquire; a missing stored
field reads 0 without an authored literal default. See `guide maintains`
for disclosure and stream cost, and `guide feeds` for Trending.
