assets, client, wire, reads, shapes, writes, programs, jobs, native, feeds, search,
effects, actions, routes, services, presence, receipts, read-only, manual-receipts, bounds, refusals, personas, testing, witness. `why
<CODE>` explains refusals.

E_QUARRY_UNSUPPORTED means the guessed construct is not a Quarry form.
For example, `a?.b` uses Quarry's null-propagating `a.b`. The
reported rewrite names the accepted spelling; `snapback4 check --fix`
applies it when marked mechanical. For a different algorithm, use the
language card's bounded loop, helper or native-job idiom. Accepting a
rewrite does not add an alias to the language. `len(x)` and `length(x)`
are accepted aliases of `count(x)` and need no rewrite.

E_ID_REUSED means the request ID already belongs to another operation or
different arguments. For example, retrying an invitation with the same ID
but a different email changes its intent. To collect or retry the original,
keep its operation, ID and raw arguments exactly; for a new invitation,
use a new ID. Explicit null and an omitted optional argument are different
raw inputs even when validation gives them the same value. See `guide
actions` for durable invocation collection and `guide writes` for mutations.

For a public Following feed, see `guide feeds`. Materialization requires
public sources with immutable mappings and owner write rules. Posts and reposts
may bound acquisition by time; public follows may sync fully, use a horizon,
or stay online only.

The compiler plans predicates, ordering, `search` and unnamed `unique` indexes
(`guide indexes`). Durations are integer milliseconds in any expression.

The public activity union below supplies each reader's private
delivered feed.

Existing explicit indexes, merges, fixed chunks, aggregates and timelines keep
their meaning. New code uses predicates, views and `for` sweeps. Following's
view declaration is shown above; `guide feeds` owns its complete example.

An unread count can use the same expiring receipts as message history. The
server reads a total plus its unswept expiry backlog (`guide maintains`).

Shapes choose the fields returned from a row or page.
Name a shape to reuse the same result layout across reads.

`{ ...p, extra: true }` copies a present row or object's known fields. Fields
can replace inherited fields: `{ ...p, handle: { value: p.handle } }` and
`p { *, handle: { value: .handle } }` return an object in place of the handle
text. The replacing field determines the generated type. A row contributes
the same columns and `pending?: boolean` as `p { *, extra: true }`.
A spread result is `pending` if any row spread into it, directly or through a
spread local, is pending, even when all of that row's fields are replaced.
Later spreads replace earlier fields from left to right. `pending` cannot be supplied or overwritten
in an object that spreads a row. This changes only the output;
rules, ordering and cursors still use the original row.
E_QUARRY_DUPLICATE_FIELD refuses two explicit fields with the same name, even
with a spread between them. Rename or remove the second field; the rewrite
names both locations. A bare column is an explicit field too.
E_QUARRY_SPREAD refuses nullable operands and values without statically known
fields. Establish the row first: `p = profiles[handle = h] ! else NOT_FOUND`,
then `return { ...p, extra: true }`.

An object spread's wildcard follows field order; when shaping an existing row shape,
explicit computed fields win over its wildcard. E_QUARRY_SHAPE_JOIN refuses
joining different row kinds, or a row-derived value and a non-row value,
at the conditional, assignment, return or collection that combines them.
Spread both row arms before joining, or build both arms with the same shape
and kind. The rule also applies inside objects and collections, even when the
result is only read by field. Identical kinds keep their existing behavior. Null adds absence to the same
kind; it does not introduce a competing wildcard rule. Resetting a collector
to `[]` keeps it empty, including inside a loop; a later append can establish
its row kind again. A nonempty unknown value cannot join a row.

Only simple conditionals or two-value reassignments of row locals or row
reads get pasteable repairs, with nullability and lazy evaluation preserved.
Reassignment edits require adjacent assignments (the second may be guarded),
with no intervening use of the reassigned local.
Coalescing, nested field conflicts, containers and helper returns instead
name the conflicting kinds and field path and explain how to make them
agree. These explanations do not suggest source edits.
Here `listing` is the expanded object, or null for a missing or hidden listing.

In the first example, table and shape names are the language card's. A shape over a page is
a bounded loop; its fields are the row's columns by bare name, `*` for all
of them, `...shape` for a named shape's fields, and `name: expr` with `.`
as the row. There is no `select` spelling.
A table-typed helper accepts that table's row or reference. A reference's
field reads its row: `.slot.day` is `slots[.slot].day`, null when missing or
hidden; `slots[.slot] ! else NOT_FOUND` refuses instead. Shapes are projections,
not declared helper-argument types.
A row-based shape keeps `pending?: boolean` from its base, including `*`, named
spreads and subsequent shapes. It is this device's unconfirmed change, absent
after confirmation; it is not a schema column or metadata on a containing record.
`guide reads` owns paging and continuation; `guide programs` owns helpers.

`shape card = { id, name, owner: .ownerId }` names a shape; `row card` and
`page card` use it, and `{ ...card, extra: 1 }` spreads its fields into
another. After a scalar predicate, `where not .hidden card` shapes the page
with the declared `card`, as does `where not .hidden { ...card }`. A valid
row/object shape inside a predicate keeps its meaning; parenthesize that
operand, or use `{ ...card }` explicitly for the page.
`fn isBrief(ttl: int ?): ttl != null` is a helper expression and
`fn stamp(roomId: rooms):` a helper block ending in `return expr` or a bare `return`,
each expanded where it is called (`isBrief(ttl)`; `stamp(r.id)` as a
statement or expression), at most eight levels deep. A table-typed helper parameter keeps a row argument as a row with fields and no lookup; a reference argument stays a reference. A helper can write only
when its caller can; a query's diagnostic names the write at the call site.
A helper's `return` ends only that call, including inside a page's shape;
the page keeps its continuation and completeness.

The rule applies only to a query's top-level returned shape expression,
`return <base> { ... }`: the base is an inline scan or merge, or a variable
with exactly one definition, that definition a read, no reassignment and no
other use anywhere in the program. The binder marks that lowered loop; only
that loop drops a row whose shape the meter starved and every later row.
`next` reaches the unfinished row first. A preceding fully computed row
supplies its exclusive position; otherwise the first unfinished rule-visible
row supplies an inclusive position — provided the page's own materialization was
not cut: a drain-cut merge with no fully computed emission, an opening cut or a
word-limit cut retains no continuation. Following an inclusive cursor that again
starves the same first row's returned shape refuses with E_SHAPE_EXCEEDS_METER
instead of returning an empty page with the same `next`: the message names the
read site and ceiling (8,192 examined rows); bound it (`first N`/`last N`) or
move it out of the returned shape. A shaped collector that is not the returned
expression keeps today's behavior: its empty or partial shape stays on the page,
with the existing continuation ownership and position, without trimming or rewind.
This includes assigned shapes, records, conditionals, helpers, aliases and
collector payloads; some such compositions have no continuation owner.
The answer stays `complete: false` on a meter cut, with `cut: 'meter'` on
devices and uniform server reads; non-uniform server reads keep `cut: null`.
A nested page's cut still makes the answer incomplete.
A collector building a returned value makes the query incomplete if it exits
with rows still unconsumed, even on a short final page.
Every page with more rows needs its own returned
cursor owner; another field's page cannot cover a lost sibling or auxiliary
page. A fully consumed, exhausted scan is complete without an owner, including
an exact-bound scan returned as `count(rows)` (subject to the meter, rules and
device horizon). An auxiliary loop over an intact returned page does not change
its completeness, even if that loop breaks. Repeating a page read never clears
an earlier loss. If an owned page site executes repeatedly, only its final
execution supplies `next`; a continuation lost by an earlier execution still
makes the query incomplete.

A program's prefix `exists` is a top-1 scan below the page: no cursor and no
page overflow. Expired siblings still cost examined rows, and `matching` pays
word discovery. A positive held row proves existence on a device regardless of
its horizon; only a negative answer past that horizon needs coverage. A
query cut is an incomplete null; a mutation cut is `E_BOUND` with no write.
Mutation prefix existence tests require a uniform plain prefix and the same
expiry admission as other scans (guide programs). Rule probes keep
exact-key, one-unit semantics. `exists` accepts predicates and seeks, but no `first`/`last` or cursor.

Types describe the values a column or argument accepts.
They also set limits on text, lists and uploaded assets.

`?` after a type makes it optional: null when absent, and an omitted
optional argument reads as null. Text literals in id positions are ids. A
`<table>` reference is a typed id, with no implicit existence check and no
delete cascade: the string `"null"` is an id, and JSON null only fits an
optional type; when a target must be visible, `require exists t[id] else
CODE` before the write (guide writes). `=`
and `!=` are total (null equals null); `<` and friends need present operands:
narrow with `if x != null:`, `x ! else CODE`, or `x ?? default`. A null guard
also narrows a bound row's field (`r.changedAt != null`), until the local is rebound. `time`
arithmetic: `time - time` is an int, `time + int` a time. Duration literals are integer milliseconds:
`now + 30s`, `now - 1d`, `500ms`, `15m` and `7d`. `/` and `%` give
the Euclidean quotient and remainder of ints or times; zero refuses `E_DIV_ZERO`.
Check the divisor first: `require n != 0 else EMPTY`.
An enum is accepted as `text <=N` only if every variant fits N characters
and contains no control characters except tab, LF and CR,
including when both types are optional. This is a static, total widening;
it adds no runtime conversion. Otherwise give the helper parameter the enum
type. `(now / 1) * 1000` explicitly scales integer milliseconds; a scaled
count belongs in an `int` column. A repeated pure `fn` call narrows under its null guard when its arguments
are names, snapshot field paths, literals or such calls. Pure helpers read
no tables or clocks and write nothing. Other optional calls still need a
local: bind once, then guard it.
Text `+` concatenates; `count(text)` counts characters. Loop-built strings and
lists are heap-bound; a write still validates their actual column lengths.

A column may end with `default <literal | now | viewer>`. Omitted insert
fields take their defaults before rules run; explicit values, including null
on an optional column, win. `now` and `viewer` use the writing host's context.
An added required column with a literal default also fills absent fields in
old images on every host, without rewriting rows or logging partition events.
Changing a required default rechecks its existing unique indexes and caps too.
`data` and `sql` show that interpretation; device persistence exports are raw storage images.
Optional columns still read null when absent. New required `default now` or
`default viewer` columns adopt only an empty table; otherwise use an optional
column or a literal default. `check` reads `.snapback4/store.sqlite` when it
exists (or `--store path`); `E_ADOPT` locates each successor refusal and its
rewrite, as `dev` refuses the save. Without a store, check only compiles.

Pages, lists and shaped collections share the list operations: `sort`, `slice`,
`count`, `sum`, `group`, `first`, `last`, `at`, `join` and `for`. Their elements
must still fit the operation: `join` joins texts; `sum(page, .amount)` projects numbers.

For complete index, rule and expiry recipes, open `guide indexes`,
`guide rules` or `guide expire` directly.
- Every table has an implicit unique `id`.

- **Types:** `principal`, `id`, `<table>` (a reference to that table's
  id), `int` (within ±(2^53 − 1); there are no floats), `time`
  (milliseconds), `bool`, `decimal <scale>`, `money <CUR> [scale]` (both
  hold integer minor units), `text`, `text <=N`, `text M..N`, each with optional
  `format handle|url`, `enum('a', 'b')`, `json <=N`, `bytes <=N`,
  `[type] <=N` (a bounded list), `image <=N [once]` and `video <=N` (an
  upload the row holds — `guide assets`); `?` after a type makes the column
  optional (null when absent). `default <literal | now | viewer>` fills an
  omitted insert column on the writing host; an explicit value wins.
  A required literal default also fills absent columns in older rows on every host; optional columns still read null when absent.
  An enum fits `text <=N` when every variant has at most N characters and
  contains no control characters except tab, LF and CR: a
  static, total widening with no runtime conversion. If any variant exceeds
  N, use the enum type on the helper parameter instead.

- **References** are typed ids, with no implicit existence check and no
  delete cascade. Any string is an id, including `""` and `"null"`; JSON
  `null` only fits an optional reference. When a mutation requires a visible target, write
  `require exists prompts[promptId] else PROMPT_NOT_FOUND` before its
  writes: a metered point read that refuses absent and hidden targets
  alike. Target deletion and dependent-row cleanup are the application's
  policy, expressed in mutations and rules.

- **Keys and search:** `unique handle` or `unique postId, principal` enforces
  a product key. Add `else HANDLE_TAKEN 'That handle is taken.'` for a visible
  collision's code and message. Named keys resolve ambiguous positional types. Use
  `search body, caption` for word-prefix search. Predicates and `by .at`
  choose access indexes automatically; `guide indexes` explains inspection
  and optional tuning. `unique principal, day(at)` gives calendar uniqueness.

- **Constraints:** `cap N by cols` (at most N rows per group; a product constraint), `immutable cols`, `after insert <- exists
  t[..]` (a row that must exist by the end of the mutation that inserted
  this one).

- **Rules:** `read`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, each `<-` one
  expression over the row (`.col`), `viewer`, and literals: `allow`,
  `deny`, `public` (or the table line `public 'reason'`, which also
  documents why), `.col = viewer`, `.col != 'x'`,
  `exists t[.a, viewer, 'literal']` (a probe may name its columns:
  `exists t[id = .docId, ownerId = viewer]`), `created t[..]` (insert rules
  only: true when this mutation inserted the probed row), `and`, `or`,
  `not`. `update (old, next) <- old.x = next.x` names both images. A table
  with no rule for an effect denies it. A rule may probe existence on an aggregate view
  over an expiring source at one unit, but `check` refuses an equality on its
  `value` (E_QUARRY_LIVE_MAINTAIN_PROBE): read the view in the program;
  its live value cannot be probed at one unit. Equalities on non-expiring
  maintains and ordinary tables are unchanged. Rules compare with `=` and `!=`
  only; the system principal consults no rules. Write authority and refusal
  disclosure are separate, as `guide writes` states.

- **Sync** (`guide sync`) and **retain**: `retain until-revoked` (the default: a
  device drops a group's rows when it leaves the group) or
  `retain delivered-history` (it keeps what it was given).

- **Expire:** `expire at .expiresAt` (a `time ?` column; its sweep index is generated). A row past that time is
  absent to every reader on every host from that moment, before any rule;
  the server sweeps on a one-second tick, at most 2,000 rows per pass, and
  the deletion streams to each device holding it. Backlog or downtime can
  delay physical deletion. A `cap` counts live rows. Its maintained physical
  count proves room when below the cap; otherwise a bounded authorization
  walk checks live occupancy. Unique checks skip expired collisions at the
  same full key. These candidates use the internal ledger described in
  `guide rules`; exhausting the shared physical allowance refuses with E_RULE.
  Secondary-key predecessors remain until the sweep.
  A row inserted already expired by a program is retired at its commit's end,
  releasing its cap occupancy without a later deletion event. Reviving it
  within that commit preserves it. Seeds and loads keep expired rows for sweep.
  Devices queue occupancy-increasing writes on expiring capped tables without
  predicted rows: even a complete live snapshot omits unswept expired rows.
  Unique checks never scan unrelated keys; a saturated cap may inspect its group.

Held device observations republish at the deadline, including offline.
  Server-answered reads use `client.now()` and `useNow(deadline)` to hide rows
  while their next answer is pending (`guide reads`).
  This is an application table, separate from the server's `connected[p]`.
  That server-decided connection signal has no `expiresAt`.
  The server will not return it again after expiry, but does not push a
  removal at that instant.
  A null time never expires. Disappearing messages
  are one field on insert, `expiresAt: now + ttl if ttl != null else
  null` with `ttl: int ?`; nothing else to write.

An ordinary maintained `view` over an
  expiring table subtracts its unswept expired backlog from the physical
  total on the server. Devices still recompute live contributions; a partial
  device reports `complete: false`. If the meter interrupts an ordinary aggregate
  lookup, backlog scan or device live group, the query returns `data: null,
  complete: false`, without substituting zero or a partial total.
  Value-order indexes over expiring sources are refused
  (`E_QUARRY_MAINTAIN_EXPIRE`): live values change before the physical sweep,
  so stored top-N can miss a winner. For a window over the entity's own
  immutable time, `guide feeds` gives a predicate over a non-expiring source. A rolling
  contribution window still needs live counts; a cut makes that answer incomplete.

E_TYPE means a runtime value has the wrong kind for the operation using it.
For example, a raw program cannot add the text `'3'` as an integer; supply
`3` as a number and compile the program against its schema. Read the
message's expected and actual types, correct seeds or wire inputs, and
use the generated API types. Changing a declaration does not convert old
values; repair the values before narrowing their type.

E_OVERFLOW means integer arithmetic left the value model's range of
−9,007,199,254,740,991 through 9,007,199,254,740,991. For example,
`9007199254740991 + 1` cannot be represented. Bound the inputs and
intermediate arithmetic before adding or multiplying. Decimal and money
columns store integer minor units in that same range; they do not provide
larger integers. For an overflowing aggregate, reduce its contributions or
split the grouping; the refusal names the view and value column without
revealing a hidden computed sum, and the failed write rolls back.

E_FIELD means a runtime field selection has no such field. For example,
a raw object `{ title: 'hello' }` has no `body`; select `title` or construct
the declared object instead. Compile the program so field names are checked,
and narrow an optional row with `row ! else NOT_FOUND` when presence is
required. Ordinary Quarry field access propagates a null base as null;
that is not evidence that the row exists.

E_QUARRY_TYPE means the expression's type does not fit its position.
The diagnostic names the expected and actual types and the source location.
A table reference is that table's typed id, not its row: `ref.field` reads
the row (`table[ref].field`, null when missing or hidden), and `table[id] !
else NOT_FOUND` refuses instead. Narrow an optional value with `if x != null:`,
`x ! else CODE` or `x ?? default` before using it where a present value is
required. Use the declared enum type when its variants cannot all widen
to the helper's text bound; changing a type never converts stored values.
